question: 世界八大奇迹中的巴比伦空中花园是什么？
subject: daily
figureAlt: 三格图解：第一格，国王为想念家乡山地的王后建花园；第二格，花园是一层层台地，下面有拱顶撑住，河水被提到最高层再往下浇；第三格，植物从台地边缘垂下来，远看像悬在空中，但遗址至今没有找到确切位置。底部说明：标准说法是古代世界七大奇迹，空中花园是其中之一，第八大奇迹只是后人的说法
oneLine: 它不是真的悬在天上，而是一座一层层升高的「梯田楼」：传说国王为了安慰想家的王后，在每层台地上种满花木，再让人把河水提到最高层，让水一层层往下浇。植物从高台边缘垂下来，远看像浮在空中。先纠正一个小地方：标准说法是「古代世界七大奇迹」，空中花园是其中之一；「第八大奇迹」只是后人形容了不起工程的说法，并不是正式名单。
points: 先把名单摆正：古代世界七大奇迹是吉萨大金字塔、巴比伦空中花园、奥林匹亚宙斯神像、以弗所阿尔忒弥斯神庙、哈利卡纳苏斯摩索拉斯陵墓、罗德岛太阳神巨像、亚历山大灯塔。空中花园是其中之一，不是「八大」。「第八大奇迹」是后来人们夸一项工程了不起时的说法，比如长城、兵马俑都被人这么叫过，但它不是古代那张正式名单。
它长什么样：传说新巴比伦国王尼布甲尼撒二世，为来自米底、想念家乡绿色山地的王后阿米蒂斯建了这座花园。它不是一盆盆花吊在空中，而是一层层升高的台地：下面用拱顶撑住，上面铺土、种树和灌木，再从幼发拉底河把水提到最高层，让水顺着渠道一层层往下浇。植物从台地边缘垂下来，远看就像悬在空中，所以叫「空中花园」。
它真的存在吗：这是七大奇迹里唯一连位置都没确认的一个。古希腊罗马作家（如贝罗苏斯、狄奥多罗斯、斯特拉波）描述过它，但在巴比伦城（今天伊拉克希拉附近）没有找到能对得上的遗址。有学者（如斯蒂芬妮·达利）认为，古代记录可能把亚述国王辛那赫里布在尼尼微修的花园记到了巴比伦头上。它可能毁于地震、战争或河床变化，也可能一半是真、一半是传说——所以最稳妥的说法是「传说中」。
followUp: 为什么现在连它的遗址都找不到？

en.question: What are the Hanging Gardens of Babylon — said to be one of the 'Eight Wonders of the World'?
en.oneLine: It was not a garden floating in mid-air, but a stepped terraced building: legend says a king built it to comfort his homesick queen, planted trees on every terrace, and had river water lifted to the top so it could flow down and water each level. Plants spilled over the edges, so from a distance it looked as if it were floating. One correction first: the standard list is the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World — the Hanging Gardens is one of them. 'Eighth wonder' is just a later phrase for an impressive feat, not an official list.
points: First, get the list right: the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World are the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Colossus of Rhodes, and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. The Hanging Gardens is one of the seven, not an 'eighth'. People later call an impressive project an 'eighth wonder' — the Great Wall and the Terracotta Army have both been described that way — but that is not the ancient official list.

What it looked like: legend says King Nebuchadnezzar II of the Neo-Babylonian Empire built it for his queen, Amytis of Media, who missed the green mountains of her homeland. It was not flowerpots hung in the air but a stack of rising terraces: vaulted arches held them up, soil and trees and shrubs were planted on top, and water was lifted from the Euphrates to the highest level, then flowed down through channels to water each terrace. Plants hung over the edges, so from a distance it seemed to float — hence the name.

Did it really exist? It is the only one of the seven whose location has never been confirmed. Greek and Roman writers such as Berossus, Diodorus and Strabo described it, but no matching ruins have been found at Babylon, near modern Hillah in Iraq. Some scholars, such as Stephanie Dalley, argue that ancient records may have credited the Assyrian king Sennacherib's gardens at Nineveh to Babylon instead. It may have been destroyed by earthquakes, war or a shifting river, or it may be half real and half legend — so the safest wording is 'according to legend'.
en.followUp: Why has no one ever found its ruins?
en.figureAlt: Three panels: a king builds a garden for a queen who misses the mountains of home; the garden is a stack of terraces held up by arches, with river water lifted to the top and poured down; plants hang over the edges so it looks suspended in the air, but its ruins have never been found. Bottom note: the standard list is the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World — the Hanging Gardens is one of them; 'eighth wonder' is only a later phrase
